old_digest: The side which bats firstand leads by 75 runs shall have the option of requiring the other side to follow their Innings
new_digest: The side which bats first and leads by 75 runs shall have the option of requiring the other side to follow their innings.

old_digest: In a One Day Match the Umpires should decide if there is sufficient time left to carry the game to a further issue after each side has completed an innings.
new_digest: If the Captains are unable to agree, the Umpires should decide if there is sufficient time left to carry the game to a further issue after each side has completed an innings.

old_digest: When there shall be less than five players on a side, Bounds shall be placed twenty-two yards each in a line from the off and leg stump. 16
new_digest: When there shall be less than five players on a side, Bounds shall be placed twenty-two yards each in a line from the off and leg stump.

old_digest: Leg Byes, nor Overthrows shall be allowed, nor shall the Striker be caught out behind the wicket, nor stumped. When there shall be less than five players on a side, neither Byes.
new_digest: When there shall be less than five players on a side, neither Byes, Leg Byes, nor Overthrows shall be allowed, nor shall the Striker be caught out behind the wicket, nor stumped.
A three days’ match between two sides of eleven players adjudged first-class shall be regarded as a first-class fixture.

old_digest: When part of the bowler’s foot is grounded on or outside the return crease the Umpire should call “No Bail.”
new_digest: When part of the bowler’s back foot is grounded on or outside the return crease the Umpire should call “No Ball.”

An “Over” should always be begun if “time” has not been reached and should be finished except as hereafter provided. If a wicket fall within two minutes of “time” the Umpires shall call “time” unless the incoming batsman claims his right to bat for the time remaining. If a wicket fall after “time” has been reached the Umpires shall call “time” If a bowler is injured so that he cannot finish the “over” he has begun, the over shall be regarded as completed.

old_digest: If one run is attempted and the batsman is run out the “No Ball” alone counts If runs are made off a “No Ball,” although the runs are scored and not the “No Ball,” the bowler is allowed another delivery.
new_digest: If one run is attempted and the batsman is run out the “No Ball” alone counts. If runs are made off a “No Ball,” although the runs are scored and not the “No Ball,” the bowler is allowed another delivery.
If the striker kicks the ball wilfully no runs shall be scored

old_digest: In 1911 an agreement was arrived at between the Counties that “Trial balls, if both batsmen are at the wickets, be not allowed in First Class Matches.’ This arrangement was approved and adopted by the M.C.C.
new_digest: In 1911 an agreement was arrived at between the Counties that “Trial balls, if both batsmen are at the wickets, be not allowed in First Class Matches. This arrangement was approved and adopted by the M.C.C.

old_digest: Where a batsman takes his guard in front of the popping crease and a run is made from that point it is not the custom for the Umpire to call “one short”. When a batsman has actually made more runs for a boundary hit than have been arranged for the boundary, this Law will prevail, and the runs completed should be scored.
new_digest: When a batsman takes his guard in front of the popping crease and a run is made from that point, the Umpire does not call ‘‘one short’’.

old_digest: The Striker is Out-

new_digest: An Umpire is justified in ruling that part of a bail had been “struck off’” if as a result of the wicket being hit any part of either bail has been disturbed from its original position on the top of the stumps.

old_digest: But if he hit the ball a second time before it touches the ground and is caught, he would be out under this Law. A Batsman would be out if caught off a ball which before striking the bat had hit his pad.
new_digest: But if he hit the ball a second time before it touches the ground and is caught, he would be out under this Law A Batsman would be out if caught off a ball which before striking the bat had hit his pad.

old_digest: Notes on Law 23 If the ball rebounds off the pads or person of the wicket-keeper, without having first touched the bat or hand oi the Striker, and the Striker is out of his ground the decision should be “Stumped,” and not “Run Out.”
new_digest: If the ball rebounds off the pads or person of the wicket-keeper, without having first touched the bat or hand of the Striker, and the Striker is out of his ground, the decision should be “Stumped,” and not “Run Out.”

old_digest: A Batsman may be out lb w, although the bowler is bowling round the wicket, if the case comes within this Law.
new_digest: A Batsman may be out l b w, although the bowler is bowling round the wicket, if the case comes within this Law.

old_digest: It is sometimes only possible for a bowler bowling round the wicket to obtain an l.b.w with a breaking ball. It is immaterial whether the ball breaks or not.
new_digest: It is immaterial whether the ball breaks or not It is sometimes only possible for a bowler bowling round the wicket to obtain an l b w with a breaking ball. The Umpire would be justified in giving the batsman out l b w if in playing at the ball the striker’s hat blew off and deflected the course of the ball which otherwise would have hit his wicket, all the requirements of Law 24 having been fulfilled.

old_digest: (See Law 16, Note 3.) * If in making a second stroke to keep a ball out of his wicket, the Striker hit down his wicket as above he would be out.
new_digest: If in making a second stroke to keep a ball out of his wicket, the Striker hit down his wicket as above he would be out.
Either Batsman is Out-

old_digest: It would not be out if the striker hit the ball into the opposite wickets—the other batsman being out of his ground—unless the nail had been touched by a fieldsman after being hit and before striking the wickets.
new_digest: It would not be out if the striker hit the ball into the opposite wickets—the other batsman being out of his ground—unless the ball had been touched by a fieldsman after being hit and before striking the wickets.

old_digest: When a run has been made oft’ a no-ball the no-ball should be scored although the ball has been caught. 12
new_digest: When a run has been made on a no-ball the run should be added to the score of the striker although the ball has been caught.

old_digest: A ball does not become “Dead” when the bails are of! or the wickets stnick down or because an unsuccessful appeal has been made to the Umpire. The ball does not become “Dead” on hitting the Umpire.
new_digest: A ball does not become “Dead” when the bails are off or the wickets struck down or because an unsuccessful appeal has been made to the Umpire. The ball does not become “dead” on merely hitting the Umpire unless it lodges in his pocket or clothing.

old_digest: A ball can only become “Dead” under Laws 33a, 336, 34, 35, 41 & 50, or on the call of a boundary.
new_digest: A ball can only become “Dead” under Laws 33a, 33b and Note 3 above, 34, 35, 41 & 50, or on the call of a boundary.

old_digest: A substitute shall be allowed to field or run between wickets for any player, who may during the match, be incapacitated from illness or injury, but for no other reason, except with the consent of the opposite side. 13 It iswcll to remember that a side which loses a player’s services through illness or injury, brought about during a match, is entitled to a substitute, “it shall be allowed” whereas under other circumstances consent isnecessaiy which must depend upon the courtesy of the opposing Captain.
new_digest: A substitute shall be allowed to field or run between wickets for any player, who may during the match be incapacitated from illness or injury, but for no other reason, except with the consent of the opposite side. It is well to remember that a side which loses a player’s services through illness or injury, brought about during a match, is entitled to a substitute, “it shall be allowed” whereas under other circumstances consent is necessary which must depend upon the courtesy of the opposing Captain.
No substitute shall be allowed to bat or bowl.

old_digest: In case any substitute shall be allowed tc run between wickets, the Striker may bo run out if either he or his substitute be out of his ground.
new_digest: In case any substitute shall be allowed to run between wickets, the Striker may be run out if either he or his substitute be out of his ground.

old_digest: The intention of this Law is that the injured striker’s ground, when he has a substitute to run for him, is at the wicket keeper’s end. lie himself can only be run out at that end as provided for in the latter part of the Law.
new_digest: The intention of this Law is that the injured striker's ground, when he has a substitute to run for him, is at the wicket keeper’s end. He himself can only be run out at that end as provided for in the latter part of the Law.

old_digest: It shall measure not less than nine inches, nor more than nine inches and one-quarter in circumference. It has become the practice to call for another ball at any time, with the Umpire’s consent, if the old one has become damaged or if the bowler has lifted the seam to obtain a better hold.
new_digest: It shall measure not less than eight and thirteen-sixteenths inches, nor more than nine inches in circumference. In the event of the Umpires agreeing that a ball in use is unfit for play they shall have power to allow another ball (as much as possible like the one discarded) to be substituted.

old_digest: The “five runs” are to be added to the runs already made when the F eldsman “wilfully” stopped the ball.

The Wicket-keeper shall stand behind the wicket If he shall take the ball for the purpose of stumping, before it has passed the wicket, or, if he shall incommode the Striker by any noise, or motion, or If any part of his person be over or before the wicket, the Striker shall not be out, excepting under Laws 26, 27, 28, 29 and 30.
new_digest: The Wicket-keeper shall stand behind the wicket. If he shall take the ball for the purpose of stumping, before it has passed the wicket, or, if he shall incommode the Striker by any noise, or motion, or if any part of his person be over or before the wicket, the Striker shall not be out, excepting under Laws 26, 27, 28, 29 and 30.

old_digest: N.B.—An appeal, “Mow’s that?” covers all ways of being out (within the jurisdiction of the Umpire appealed to), unless a* specific way of getting out is stated by the person asking.
new_digest: N.B.—An appeal, “How’s that?” covers all ways of being out (within the jurisdiction of the Umpire appealed to), unless a specific way of getting out is stated by the person asking.

old_digest: (See Notes under “The Batsman,” page 16.)
new_digest: (See Note 3 under “The Batsman,” page 15.)

old_digest: No act on the part of the fielding side can cause a batsman to be out after the Umpire has called “Over,” but an appeal may be made within the allotted time. 15
new_digest: No act on the part of the fielding side can cause a batsman to be out after the Umpire has called “Over,” but an appeal may be made within the allotted time.

old_digest: The side which bats first and leads by 150 runs in a threedays’ match, or by 100 runs in a two days’ match, shall have the option of requiring the other side to follow their innings.
new_digest: The side which bats first and leads by 150 runs (in Australia 200 runs) in a match of three days or more, or by 100 runs in a two days’ match, shall have the option of requiring the other side to follow their innings.

old_digest: The In-side may declare their innings at an end In a three days’ match, at any time on the second day; in a two days’ match the Captain of the batting side has power to declare his innings at a close at any time; but such declaration may not be made on the first day later than 1 hour and 40 minutes before the hour agreed on for drawing stumps; in a one day match at any time.
new_digest: The In-side may declare their innings at an end in a match of three days or more, at any time on the second day; in a two days’ match the Captain of the batting side has power to declare his innings at a close at any time; but such declaration may not be made on the first day later than 1 hour and 40 minutes before the hour agreed on for drawing stumps; in a one day match at any time. If a side declare its innings during the luncheon interval, it must do so within fifteen minutes after the commencement of such interval otherwise an extra seven minutes will be allowed for rolling. old_digest: Each wicket shall be eight inches in width, and consist of three stumps, with two bails upon the top. The stumps shall be of equal and of sufficient size to prevent the ball from passing through, twenty-seven inches out of the ground. The bails shall be each four inches in length, and when in position, on the top of the stumps, shall not project more than half-an-inch above them.
new_digest: Each wicket shall be not less than eight inches nor more than nine inches in width, and consist of three stumps, with two bails upon the top. The stumps shall be of equal and of sufficient size to prevent the ball from passing through, not less than twenty-seven inches nor more than twenty-eight inches out of the ground. The bails shall be each not less than four inches nor more than four inches and a half in length, and when in position, on the top of the stumps, shall not project more than half-an-inch above them. In all first class cricket and in all matches in which teams selected by Governing Bodies of Cricket are engaged, each wicket shall be nine inches in width, the stumps twenty-eig ...
The distance shall be 4 feet from the centre of the stumps to the inside edge of the popping crease.

old_digest: The Ground shall not be rolled, watered, covered, mown, or beaten during a match, except before the commencement of each innings and of each day's play, when, unless the In-Side object, the ground shall be swept and rolled for not more than ten minutes. In week end starts the wicket may be mown on the Monday morning under the supervision of the Umpires. The batting side has a right to have the ground swept and rolled “for not more than 10 minutes” immediately before the commencement of each innings and of each day’s play. In week-end starts the wicket shall be mown, under the supervision of the Umpires, on the first day on which the match is resumed.
